summary: Covers fundamental data representations in C including basic types (int, float, double, char), type modifiers (unsigned, signed, short, long), identifier rules and case sensitivity, variable declarations vs definitions, multiple declarations in a single line, constants using #define vs the const qualifier, sizeof operator, escape sequences, and conversion specifiers in formatted I/O.

key_terms.definition: A named location in computer memory that holds a value which can be retrieved and modified during execution.
A token composed of letters, digits, and underscores that does not begin with a digit and is not a reserved keyword.
A reserved word in C that has a fixed grammatical meaning to the compiler and cannot be redefined by the programmer.
An immutable value defined either via the preprocessor #define directive or with the const type qualifier.
A placeholder in a format control string (such as %d, %f, %c) instructing printf or scanf how to format or interpret data.
The automatic discarding of fractional parts when a floating-point value is assigned to an integer variable.
A unary operator that returns the memory address of its operand, required when reading primitive scalars with scanf.
An identifier defined by #define that is substituted textually by the preprocessor before compilation begins.
A character combination beginning with a backslash (\) used to represent non-printing or control characters such as newline (\n) and tab (\t).
A compile-time unary operator that returns the memory size in bytes required to store an object or type.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct way to declare a float variable in C?
questions.explanation: In C, declaring a single-precision floating-point variable requires the keyword 'float' followed by a valid identifier and a statement terminator semicolon (;). 'float x();' declares a function prototype taking no specified arguments and returning float.

why_wrong.1: 'int x;' declares an integer variable, not a floating-point variable.
why_wrong.2: 'float x();' declares a function prototype that returns float, not a variable.
why_wrong.3: 'double x;' declares a double-precision floating-point variable, which typically occupies 8 bytes rather than the standard 4-byte float.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q1; Deitel Ch 2.3

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid C keyword?
questions.explanation: 'return' is one of the 32 standard C keywords defined in ANSI C89/ISO C99. 'main' is a standard function name, 'printf' is a standard library function in stdio.h, and 'integer' is not a C keyword (the keyword is 'int').

why_wrong.0: 'main' is the standard identifier where execution begins, but it is an identifier, not a reserved C keyword.
why_wrong.2: 'printf' is an external function provided by the C Standard I/O library (<stdio.h>), not a keyword.
why_wrong.3: 'integer' does not exist in C syntax; the keyword for integer types is 'int'.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q2; Deitel Fig 2.15

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct way to declare multiple integer variables in a single line?
questions.explanation: Multiple variables of the same type can be declared in a single statement by separating each identifier with a comma and ending the statement with a semicolon: 'int x, y, z;'.

why_wrong.1: 'int x; y; z;' is invalid because 'y;' and 'z;' are treated as separate statements where y and z lack type specifiers.
why_wrong.2: 'int x y z;' is a syntax error because whitespace alone cannot separate identifier tokens in a declaration list.
why_wrong.3: Colons are used in bit-field declarations and labels, not for separating variable names.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q24; Deitel Ch 2.3

questions.question: Which of the following is correct for defining a symbolic constant using the preprocessor in C?
questions.explanation: Preprocessor directives begin with '#' and do not use an assignment operator '=' or a terminating semicolon. The standard syntax is '#define IDENTIFIER replacement_text'.

why_wrong.1: 'const PI = 3.14;' lacks a type specifier (such as double or float). In standard C99/C11, explicit types are mandatory.
why_wrong.2: Preprocessor directives must begin with the '#' symbol; 'define' without '#' causes a compiler error.
why_wrong.3: 'constant' is not a C keyword.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q26; Deitel Ch 2.3

questions.question: Which of the following is correct syntax to declare a constant integer in C?
questions.explanation: In C, both 'const int x = 5;' and 'int const x = 5;' declare a type-checked read-only integer variable using the const qualifier. Additionally, '#define x 5' creates a preprocessor symbolic constant. Therefore, all three are valid mechanisms.

why_wrong.0: While valid, it is not the only correct option; both 'int const' and '#define' are also valid.
why_wrong.1: While valid ('const' can appear before or after the type specifier), options A and C are also valid.
why_wrong.2: While '#define' defines an integer literal replacement, const declarations are also valid.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q38; Deitel Ch 2.3

questions.question: What will be the exact output of the following C program?
questions.explanation: When the floating-point literal 5.95 is assigned to the integer variable 'a', C performs implicit truncation (discarding the fractional part), resulting in 5 (no rounding). The integer 2 assigned to float 'b' becomes 2.0f, and '%.1f' prints it with 1 decimal place as 2.0.

why_wrong.1: C integer assignment does NOT round up to 6; it strictly truncates toward zero.
why_wrong.2: '%.1f' requires printing one decimal digit, so it outputs '2.0', not '2'.
why_wrong.3: Implicit narrowing conversions are standard in C and generate at most a warning, not a compilation error.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C program?
questions.explanation: #define performs pure textual replacement before compilation. 'VALUE * 4' expands literally to '5 + 2 * 4'. Due to operator precedence, multiplication occurs before addition: 2 * 4 = 8, and 5 + 8 = 13. To obtain 28, the macro definition must be parenthesized: '#define VALUE (5 + 2)'.

why_wrong.0: 28 is the classic trap assuming (5 + 2) is evaluated first. Without parentheses, macro substitution is raw text: 5 + 2 * 4.
why_wrong.2: 20 would occur if (5 * 4) were evaluated, ignoring + 2.
why_wrong.3: The syntax is completely valid C.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C program?
questions.explanation: In C, character literals are integral values representing ASCII codes. 'B' has ASCII code 66. Adding 2 yields 68. Format specifier '%c' interprets 68 as character 'D', while '%d' prints the numerical value 68.

why_wrong.1: 66 is 'B'; 'B' + 2 evaluates to 68 ('D').
why_wrong.2: '%d' prints a decimal integer, not the character representation.
why_wrong.3: Character arithmetic is fully defined in C and widely tested.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C program?
questions.explanation: In C, integer literals with prefix '0x' or '0X' are hexadecimal (0x1A = 1*16 + 10 = 26). Integer literals starting with a leading '0' are octal (012 = 1*8 + 2 = 10). Both are printed in decimal via '%d'.

why_wrong.1: '%d' outputs decimal numbers, not literal string tokens like '1A'.
why_wrong.2: Octal 012 is base-8 (1*8 + 2 = 10), not decimal 12.
why_wrong.3: 0x1A is 26, not 16.

questions.question: What is guaranteed by the ISO C standard to be the output of the following code snippet?
questions.explanation: By definition in the ISO C Standard, sizeof(char) is ALWAYS exactly 1. All other data type sizes in C are expressed as multiples of the size of char.

why_wrong.0: 4 is typical for int or float, not char.
why_wrong.3: While int and pointer sizes are architecture-dependent, sizeof(char) is strictly guaranteed by the standard to be 1.

questions.question: What is the output of the following printf statement in C?
questions.explanation: The escape sequence \" prints a literal double quote ("), and \\ prints a literal single backslash (\). Thus, "\"A\\B\"\n" outputs: "A\B" followed by a newline.

why_wrong.1: The backslashes act as escape indicators and are not printed verbatim when preceding '"' or '\'.
why_wrong.2: The escaped quotes are printed; they are not stripped.
why_wrong.3: The single backslash between A and B is printed.

questions.question: Which of the following is an INVALID variable identifier in C?
questions.explanation: In C, identifiers must begin with an alphabetic letter (a-z, A-Z) or an underscore (_). They cannot begin with a numeric digit. Therefore, '3rd_student' is lexical syntax error.

why_wrong.1: Identifiers may legally begin with an underscore (_).
why_wrong.2: Digits are allowed anywhere in an identifier except as the very first character.
why_wrong.3: Uppercase letters are valid; C identifiers are case-sensitive.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between a signed int and an unsigned int in C?
options: unsigned int can only represent non-negative numbers, doubling the maximum positive range compared to signed int.
unsigned int takes up more memory bytes than signed int.
signed int cannot represent negative numbers.
unsigned int can store floating-point fractions.
questions.explanation: Both signed int and unsigned int occupy the same amount of memory (typically 4 bytes). However, an unsigned int reinterprets the most significant sign bit as a magnitude bit, shifting the range from [-2^31, 2^31 - 1] to [0, 2^32 - 1].

why_wrong.1: They occupy identical storage size (typically 32 bits).
why_wrong.2: signed int explicitly represents both positive and negative values.
why_wrong.3: Neither int type stores floating-point fractions; both are integer types.

questions.question: Is the following statement True or False? In C, identifiers may begin with an underscore (_), but cannot begin with a number.
options: True, because the lexical rules permit letters and underscores as the first character, but digits are prohibited in the initial position.
False, because underscores are strictly reserved for compiler internals and cause a syntax error if written by the programmer.
False, because modern C allows identifiers to start with digits provided they contain letters.
True, but only in variable names, not function names.
why_options: C lexical grammar specifies an identifier as (letter | '_')(letter | digit | '_')*.
Programmer identifiers can start with '_', though it is discouraged to avoid collisions with system libraries.
Identifiers starting with digits are interpreted by the lexical analyzer as numeric constants, causing syntax errors.
The identifier syntax rules apply universally to variable, function, and struct names.
questions.explanation: In C, valid identifiers consist of letters, digits, and underscores, but the first character must strictly be a letter or an underscore. An initial digit would cause the tokenizer to treat the token as a numeric constant.

why_wrong.1: Underscores are legally allowed at the start of programmer identifiers, though not recommended for library reasons.
why_wrong.2: No version of C permits identifiers to begin with digits.
why_wrong.3: The lexical rules apply identically to all identifiers in C.

questions.source: Deitel Ch 2.3; ANSI C Standard Section 6.4.2

questions.question: What is the single-character conversion specifier (excluding the percent sign) used in printf to output a single character in C?
questions.explanation: '%c' is the format specifier for printing or reading a single character in C. For example: printf("%c", 'Z');.

questions.question: Which format conversion specifier is used in scanf to read a double-precision floating-point number (double) from standard input?
questions.explanation: In scanf, '%lf' (long float) must be used to read into a variable of type double, whereas '%f' is used for float. In printf, both float and double can use '%f' due to default argument promotions.

questions.question: Identify the critical runtime bug in the following C code that causes undefined behavior or a segmentation fault:
options: scanf is missing the address operator (&) before variable 'age', passing uninitialized garbage as a memory address.
The format specifier '%d' cannot be used with int in scanf.
The variable 'age' must be declared as float before calling scanf.
printf cannot follow scanf without an intervening fflush(stdin).
questions.explanation: The function scanf requires pointer arguments indicating where to store input values. Writing 'scanf("%d", age);' passes the current uninitialized value of 'age' (garbage) as a memory pointer, causing scanf to write to an arbitrary memory address resulting in undefined behavior or a segmentation fault. The correct call is 'scanf("%d", &age);'.

why_wrong.1: '%d' is the exact conversion specifier for integer types.
why_wrong.2: 'age' is an integer quantity; declaring it as float would conflict with '%d'.
why_wrong.3: fflush(stdin) is undefined behavior in standard C and unnecessary here.

questions.question: Fill in the correct C keywords in the blank positions:
questions.template: To declare a variable that holds whole numbers, use the keyword [[blank]], whereas for numbers with single-precision decimal points, use [[blank]]. To create a read-only variable whose value cannot be reassigned, qualify the declaration with [[blank]].
questions.explanation: 'int' denotes standard whole numbers, 'float' single-precision floating-point numbers, and 'const' declares an immutable type qualifier.

questions.question: Match each C data type / concept with its standard characteristics on modern 32/64-bit systems:

pairs.right: Smallest addressable unit, typically 1 byte (8 bits), stores ASCII codes
Standard integer type, typically 4 bytes (32 bits), format %d
Double-precision floating-point, typically 8 bytes, format %lf in scanf
Enforces compiler-checked immutability on a variable

questions.explanation: In standard C, char is guaranteed to be 1 byte, int is typically 4 bytes on 32/64-bit architectures, double provides 64-bit precision, and const designates read-only memory objects.

questions.question: Order the lifecycle steps of a C variable from source definition to value retrieval:
steps: Specify variable name and data type in declaration
Compiler allocates memory storage at a specific address
Initialize variable with an initial value or input via scanf
Retrieve or evaluate variable value in expressions or printf
questions.explanation: A variable must first be declared/defined with a type and identifier. The compiler allocates its memory offset. It is then initialized (or written into), and subsequently read during expressions or output.

questions.question: Compare and contrast defining a constant using '#define MAX 100' versus 'const int MAX = 100;'. Explain at least two key technical differences.
questions.answer:
1. Mechanism: #define is a preprocessor macro directive that performs blind textual replacement before compilation without type checking or allocating memory. 'const int' creates a real, typed variable placed in read-only storage and enforced by the compiler's type system.
2. Scope & Debugging: #define has file scope from the point of definition until #undef, ignoring block scopes, and the symbol does not appear in debugger symbol tables. 'const int' respects C block scope and is visible to symbolic debuggers.
3. Address: A const variable has a memory address (&MAX), whereas a literal substituted by #define has no memory address.
marking_points: Explains that #define is a preprocessor text replacement without type checking
Explains that const int is a compiler-enforced typed read-only variable
Mentions scoping differences or debugger visibility or addressability (&)
questions.explanation: Understanding the difference between preprocessor textual replacement and compiler type-qualified const variables is a foundational concept tested in university C programming exams.

questions.question: Write a complete C main function that declares three variables: an integer 'units' initialized to 45, a float 'rate' initialized to 12.5f, and a float 'total'. Calculate 'total = units * rate' and print the result using printf formatted to 2 decimal places.
marking_points: Correctly declares int units = 45 and float rate = 12.5f
Uses printf with '%.2f' format specifier to output 2 decimal places
questions.explanation: Demonstrates declaration, mixed-type arithmetic promotion (int promotes to float during multiplication), and precise float formatting with '%.2f'.

questions.question: What is the output of the following C program?
questions.explanation: In C, variable evaluation is by value at the moment the statement runs. Variable 'c' receives 10 + 20 = 30. Modifying 'a = 5' afterwards has no effect on 'c'. The output is '30 5'.

why_wrong.1: 'c' does not dynamically recompute when 'a' is modified.
why_wrong.2: 'a' was reassigned to 5 before printing.
why_wrong.3: Sequential assignment statements are completely valid in C.

questions.question: What will be printed by the following code on a system with 8-bit two's-complement signed char?
questions.explanation: In an 8-bit two's-complement system, signed char ranges from -128 to +127 (binary 01111111). Incrementing by 1 produces binary 10000000, which evaluates to -128 in standard two's-complement rollover.

why_wrong.1: 128 cannot fit in a signed 8-bit char whose maximum value is 127.
why_wrong.2: 0 would only occur on overflow of an unsigned char at 255.
why_wrong.3: While signed overflow is technically undefined in ISO C, on GCC x86/ARM hardware with standard two's complement it yields -128.

questions.question: What is the problem with the declaration 'int a = b = c = 10;' inside a C function if b and c were not previously declared?
options: Compilation error: 'b' and 'c' are undeclared identifiers.
It is completely valid in ANSI C and initializes all three to 10.
Only 'a' is initialized to 10; 'b' and 'c' are initialized to 0.
It compiles but causes a runtime crash.
questions.explanation: In C, you cannot chain assignment initialization for variables that have not yet been declared in that statement. 'int a = b = c = 10;' attempts to evaluate 'c = 10', but 'c' has no type declaration. The correct C syntax is: 'int a = 10, b = 10, c = 10;' or declaring them first.

why_wrong.1: C requires explicit type declarations for all identifiers before use.
why_wrong.2: The compiler rejects the statement at compile time before any runtime execution.
why_wrong.3: It is a compile-time failure, not a runtime crash.

questions.question: What will be printed by the following C program?
questions.explanation: In standard C (unlike C++), character constants like 'A' have type int, so sizeof('A') == sizeof(int) (typically 4 bytes). A string literal "A" is an array of 2 chars: 'A' and the terminating null character '\0', so sizeof("A") == 2.

why_wrong.1: 'A' is an integer character constant in C (sizeof(int)), not sizeof(char).
why_wrong.2: In C++, sizeof('A') is 1, but in C it is sizeof(int) (typically 4). Also "A" includes the null terminator (2 bytes).
why_wrong.3: "A" contains 2 bytes ('A' + '\0'), not 1.

questions.question: Which conversion specifier is used in printf to print an integer in unsigned hexadecimal format using lowercase letters (a-f)?
questions.explanation: '%x' prints an integer in unsigned hexadecimal using lowercase letters (a-f). '%X' uses uppercase letters (A-F), '%o' prints in octal, and '%h' is a length modifier for short, not a standalone conversion specifier.

why_wrong.1: '%h' is a length modifier (e.g. %hd for short int), not a conversion specifier.
why_wrong.2: '%X' prints hex digits in uppercase (A-F).
why_wrong.3: '%o' prints in octal (base 8).

questions.front: What is the size and format specifier of a standard 'char' in C?
questions.explanation: Guaranteed by the ISO C standard to have sizeof(char) == 1.
questions.question: What is the size and format specifier of a standard 'char' in C?

questions.back: No. They are standard identifiers (a function name and a library function), NOT reserved language keywords.
questions.explanation: Keywords are reserved syntax words like int, return, if, while.
questions.question: Are 'main' and 'printf' keywords in C?
questions.answer: No. They are standard identifiers (a function name and a library function), NOT reserved language keywords.

questions.front: What are the rules for a valid C identifier?
questions.back: Consists of letters, digits, and underscores (_). Must NOT begin with a digit. Must NOT be a C keyword. Case-sensitive.
questions.explanation: E.g. '_count1' is valid, '1count' is invalid.
questions.question: What are the rules for a valid C identifier?
questions.answer: Consists of letters, digits, and underscores (_). Must NOT begin with a digit. Must NOT be a C keyword. Case-sensitive.

questions.front: What happens if you place a semicolon after a #define directive? (e.g. #define PI 3.14;)
questions.back: The semicolon becomes part of the replacement text, causing unexpected syntax errors in expressions (e.g. x = PI * 2 becomes x = 3.14; * 2).
questions.explanation: Preprocessor macros do not use semicolons.
questions.question: What happens if you place a semicolon after a #define directive? (e.g. #define PI 3.14;)
questions.answer: The semicolon becomes part of the replacement text, causing unexpected syntax errors in expressions (e.g. x = PI * 2 becomes x = 3.14; * 2).

questions.front: What is the difference between float and double in C?
questions.back: Float is single-precision (~6 decimal digits, typically 4 bytes, %f). Double is double-precision (~15 decimal digits, typically 8 bytes, %lf in scanf).
questions.explanation: Double provides higher precision and wider exponent range.
questions.question: What is the difference between float and double in C?
questions.answer: Float is single-precision (~6 decimal digits, typically 4 bytes, %f). Double is double-precision (~15 decimal digits, typically 8 bytes, %lf in scanf).

questions.front: Why does scanf require the '&' operator for scalar variables?
questions.back: '&' passes the variable's memory address (pointer), allowing scanf to store user input directly into that memory location.
questions.explanation: C passes arguments by value; passing the address is how scanf modifies caller memory.
questions.question: Why does scanf require the '&' operator for scalar variables?
questions.answer: '&' passes the variable's memory address (pointer), allowing scanf to store user input directly into that memory location.

questions.front: What is the effect of the 'unsigned' modifier on an integer?
questions.back: It restricts the variable to non-negative numbers, doubling the positive range (e.g. 0 to 4,294,967,295 for 32-bit int) and uses format specifier %u.
questions.explanation: The sign bit is treated as a magnitude bit.
questions.question: What is the effect of the 'unsigned' modifier on an integer?
questions.answer: It restricts the variable to non-negative numbers, doubling the positive range (e.g. 0 to 4,294,967,295 for 32-bit int) and uses format specifier %u.

questions.front: What value does an uninitialized local variable hold in C?
questions.back: Indeterminate 'garbage' value (whatever random bits currently reside in that allocated stack memory).
questions.explanation: Local (automatic) variables are not zero-initialized by default in C.
questions.question: What value does an uninitialized local variable hold in C?
questions.answer: Indeterminate 'garbage' value (whatever random bits currently reside in that allocated stack memory).

case_studies.title: Nile Student Bursary Billing Engine
case_studies.scenario: A software engineering student at Nile University is commissioned to write a billing module in C that computes semester tuition fees. The module accepts an integer number of credit units, a float tuition rate per unit, and a constant university administrative fee of 25,000 Naira defined using #define. During early code testing, calculations produce strange negative numbers and incorrect decimal figures due to variable typing and format specifier mistakes.

sub_questions.question: If 'units' is declared as an unsigned int and assigned 18, and 'rate' is float assigned 12000.50f, what data type does the expression (units * rate) evaluate to during computation?
sub_questions.explanation: Under C's usual arithmetic conversions (type promotions), when an integer operand meets a floating-point operand, the integer is implicitly converted to float before the multiplication is executed.

why_wrong.1: The integer promotes to float to prevent loss of precision.
why_wrong.2: Neither operand is double, so promotion stops at float.
why_wrong.3: Integer types promote upward to floating types in mixed arithmetic.

sub_questions.question: The student wrote '#define ADMIN_FEE 25000;' with a trailing semicolon. What happens when the compiler encounters 'total = tuition + ADMIN_FEE * 2;'?
options: It expands to 'total = tuition + 25000; * 2;', resulting in a syntax error.
The compiler automatically discards the semicolon during preprocessing.
It computes correctly because semicolons in macros are ignored.
It compiles cleanly but ignores the multiplication.
sub_questions.explanation: Preprocessor macros do not strip punctuation. The text '25000;' replaces ADMIN_FEE verbatim, producing 'total = tuition + 25000; * 2;', which is an illegal syntax error on the stray '* 2;'.

why_wrong.1: The preprocessor does not parse C syntax or strip semicolons; it is a mechanical string replacer.
why_wrong.2: Semicolons are never ignored by the preprocessor.
why_wrong.3: It fails at the compilation stage immediately following preprocessing.

sub_questions.question: The developer tests the following snippet for calculating unit discount. What is printed?
sub_questions.explanation: Both 'registered_units' (15) and 'min_threshold' (20) are integers. Therefore, 15 / 20 performs integer division, which evaluates to 0 (truncated). Only after the integer division is 0 promoted to float 0.00f. To get 0.75, cast one operand: (float)registered_units / min_threshold.

why_wrong.1: 0.75 is the classic student trap! Integer division truncates before float assignment.
why_wrong.2: 15 / 20 does not round up to 1; C truncates toward zero.
why_wrong.3: This is completely valid C syntax.

case_studies.title: Embedded Microcontroller Sensor Register Mapping
case_studies.scenario: In a lab project at Nile University, students configure an 8-bit sensor reading temperature and status flags. The sensor register returns a signed 8-bit character value, an unsigned 16-bit timestamp, and an integer calibration constant.

sub_questions.question: An unsigned char variable holds sensor raw flags. What is the valid range of numerical values an 8-bit unsigned char can store?
sub_questions.explanation: An 8-bit byte has 2^8 = 256 distinct bit patterns. Without a sign bit (unsigned), the range is 0 to 2^8 - 1, which is 0 to 255. A signed char stores -128 to +127.

why_wrong.1: -128 to 127 is the range of a signed 8-bit char (two's complement).
why_wrong.2: Unsigned values cannot store negative numbers.
why_wrong.3: 0 to 65535 is the range of a 16-bit unsigned short or integer.

sub_questions.question: What is the exact output of the following C code snippet on a standard two's complement system?
sub_questions.explanation: A signed char has range -128 to +127. 127 in binary is 01111111. Adding 1 produces 10000000, which in two's complement arithmetic represents -128.

why_wrong.1: 128 exceeds the positive range of a signed 8-bit integer.
why_wrong.2: 0 would only occur if overflowing 255 in an unsigned 8-bit type.
why_wrong.3: Signed integer overflow in C is an arithmetic rollover on two's complement systems.
